chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
title: Charlie Parker in Kansas City and the Moten versus Basie beat
summary: At Wehnwood Beach she heard Parker playing with Andy Kirk's wife, and the boys did not understand him. Kansas City wanted a steady swing; Basie lightened Moten's beat.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Do you remember when you first met Charlie Parker?

When we were working at Wehnwood Beach we'd go by where he was playing with Andy Kirk's wife, Mary, who was a very good pianist, but she had the old style... and Charlie Parker was playing just the way he did when he was in New York and it sounded funny to the boys. They'd say, "I don't know what that alto player's playing." "He sounds good but I don't know what he's doing." The two combinations together were really funny.
I asked you this before, but did the people in general in Kansas City understand what Charlie was doing?

I don't think so... because Kansas City even to now is a little back on the modern era, and to really go over big in Kansas City you have to swing. It was kind of like a slapstick thing. Therefore a small audience of modern jazz lovers but not as big as would like the Count Basie style of playing.
Of course back in the days that you're talking about which was the late 20's or early 30's approximately, what Charlie Parker was doing was so utterly outlandish, compared to -
He leave had to in Kansas City, because everything you had to have a strong beat, like Fats Waller swinging thing.

As I recall, the bands that had a very solid beat like, for example, the Bennie Moten band, some of the earlier records of the Bennie Moten band, are very... but once Basie and Walter Page and some of those people came in about 1930, the sound changed decidedly. It was lighter.
